units.unit: The student is trying to understand Hong Kong's rent control for subdivided units.
The student wants sources on how rent caps affect housing supply.
The student wants sources on what alternatives exist.
The student's claim is that a hard cap on initial rents would shrink SDU supply and hurt the newest tenants most.
A source would need to show a measured or modelled supply response to a rent cut.
The source should ideally have numbers for Hong Kong.
The source should include a real-world case like Berlin.
The student wants something on alternatives, like a rent band instead of a hard cap.
The Hong Kong numbers are doing the heavier work because a local elasticity or modelled scenario shows the effect on this exact market.
The outside case can only illustrate the mechanism.
The source should give an estimated supply elasticity or a modelled household-displacement figure for Hong Kong itself.
Hong Kong elasticity numbers, the Berlin case, stock data, the legal alternative, and the NGO survey all directly support the supply and alternatives claims.
The student wants to check the enforcement side next: how many units inspectors actually reach.
The student wants to know whether the most vulnerable tenants (no written agreement, newest arrivals) are the ones the system misses.
The student asks for documents on inspection capacity or a tenancy register.
The student needs a document showing inspectors' actual reach over the stock.
The student needs something on why tenants without written agreements or the newest arrivals are least likely to complain.
Anything on a tenancy register or inspection capacity would help.
The student needs inspection capacity and vulnerable tenant evidence.
The student notes that the inspection capacity and vulnerable tenant evidence are already unlocked.
The student still needs the other sources the draft leans on that they haven't opened.
The student lists the Berlin-style listing effects source.
The student lists the New York first-rent regulation and 2019 tightening source.
The student lists the Basic Law compensation risk source.
The student lists the Association's submission.
The student lists the consultation document's rent-band package.
The student lists the primer's point on who the newcomers are.
The claim that most needs backing is that a hard cap would push out the very people it's meant to protect: new arrivals and newly formed households.
A source would need to show who actually gets displaced when supply contracts, ideally with numbers on arrivals or household formation.
The student asks whether there is a policy brief or overview laying out who the SDU population actually is.
Before displacement numbers mean anything, the student needs the overview establishing who the SDU population actually is.
The overview should establish whether the SDU population is mostly new arrivals and newly formed households.
The student asks for a primer or policy brief on SDU demographics.
The student notes that all the needed sources are already unlocked and needed for the displacement and demographics claims.

Still needs sources on Berlin listing effects, New York first-rent regulation and 2019 tightening, Basic Law compensation risk, the Association's submission, the consultation document's rent-band package, and someone speaking to new arrivals' willingness to accept any rent for a shorter queue
For Berlin, the claim is that a hard cap shrinks listings rather than protecting renters because owners move flats to uncontrolled segments
The Berlin source would need to show initial-offer rents falling while the count of regulated listings drops within a year or so
Needs Berlin listing effects, New York first-rent and 2019 tightening, and compensation risk
Still needs the consultation document floating the floor-standard plus rent band package
Still needs the Association submission arguing compensation risk
Still needs the Basic Law compensation passages
Still needs the tenant who says he'd accept any rent for a shorter queue
The consultation document is for the claim that a banded approach has political legs
The Association's submission is for the litigation risk point
The Basic Law passages are for the same legal claim
The tenant quote is for the point that quantity, not price, is the binding constraint
All four cited documents are needed for the political, legal and queue claims
The legal opinion argues a published, indexed per-square-foot band on initial rents can be defended as rate-capping rather than confiscation
The NGO report backs tenure security plus a light band on initial rents while opposing a hard cap
The NGO survey found 61 percent would trade a nominal rent increase for three-year tenure security and 74 percent for a faster public-housing offer
A band needs survey infrastructure that doesn't exist yet, and enforcement lags without a register, but both are buildable
The working paper's displaced households are mostly new arrivals and newly formed households
That displaced group is exactly the group the policy is meant to protect
Wants to confirm the working paper really says the displaced are mostly new arrivals and newly formed households
Wants to confirm D1p2 backs the idea that's the group policy is meant to protect
Wants to re-read D1p2 to see exactly what it says about who lives in SDUs and why
D1p2 is just the primer describing who lives in SDUs and why they end up there
D1p2 doesn't say anything about who a policy is 'meant to protect'; that was the student's inference
Should drop or reword that sentence rather than pretend D1p2 supports it
D6p4 does name the 3,000–4,000 a year as mostly new arrivals and newly formed households, so that part stands
Will mark it as the student's own inference: displaced households are mostly new arrivals and newly formed households, and protecting those newcomers is the aim the student would argue for
Everything else in the essay is now grounded in what the student actually read
